'''Marian L. Palmer Capps''' (also known as '''Mrs John Winston Capps''', 1901 – November 17, 2001) was an American mathematician who became a professor at [[Norfolk State University]] and president of the Women's Auxiliary to the [[National Medical Association]].

==Education and career==
Capps was African-American,{{r|bwm|hjr}} originally from [[Norfolk, Virginia]]. After graduating from [[Booker T. Washington High School (Virginia)|Booker T. Washington High School]] in Norfolk, she earned a bachelor's degree in mathematics from [[Howard University]] in 1927.{{r|hjr}}<ref>Howard University, ''[https://hustorage.wrlc.org/disk1/ybkflip/dhu.hua.ybk_1927/mobile/ Bison]'' (1927 yearbook).</ref> Later, she earned a master's degree and Ph.D. in mathematics and mathematics education; sources differ on whether these graduate degrees were from [[Columbia University]], the [[University of Wisconsin–Madison]], or the [[Catholic University of America]].{{r|bwm|hjr|wed}} In 1938, she married John Winston Capps, then teaching at Washington High School and later a Navy radiologist.{{r|wed|john}}

She became an instructor at the [[Hampton Institute]], a [[Historically black colleges and universities|historically black college]] in [[Hampton, Virginia]],{{r|bwm|wed|award}} and eventually chaired the mathematics department there.{{r|bwm|award}} In 1956, she was listed as a professor of education at the [[South Carolina State College]].{{r|jne}} By 1959, she became a professor at [[Norfolk State University]],{{r|aaas}} where she taught for 25 years.{{r|hjr}}

==Service==
Capps served as president of the Women's Auxiliary to the [[National Medical Association]] for 1968–1969, setting a presidential theme of "Focusing on Problems of Dynamic Dimensions—Medical Careers, Mental Health, Sex Education".{{r|pres}} She led the Auxiliary in a boycott against the [[American Can Company]] for discrimination against African-Americans, and in joining an umbrella group of societies of African-American women.{{r|boycott}}

She was appointed to the Virginia State Council of Higher Education in 1978,{{r|bwm}} becoming the first African-American woman on the council. She also became the first African-American woman on the board of the [[Eastern Virginia Medical School]].{{r|hjr}}

She was active in the [[Delta Sigma Theta]] sorority, becoming in 1929 the founding president of what became the Norfolk Alumnae Chapter of the sorority and for many years afterward the national treasurer.{{r|hjr|dst}} She was also one of the first members of The Moles, a [[African-American upper class#Social and family organizations|prominent African-American women's social group]].{{r|hjr|moles}}

==Recognition==
In 1959, Capps was named a Fellow of the [[American Association for the Advancement of Science]].{{r|aaas}}

The Urban League of Hampton Roads, a society devoted to African-American social and economic issues that Capps helped found, offers an annual award named for Capps for outstanding contributions to the league's causes through educational activities.{{r|award}}
